items.stem: Define the term 'personal data'.
items.answer: Data that relates to a living person who can be identified from it, such as name, address, date of birth or medical records.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Data that relates to a living person who can be identified from it, such as name, address, date of birth or medical records. [2]

items.stem: Explain why sensitive personal data needs more protection than other personal data.
items.answer: It could be used to discriminate against or harm the person (e.g. health or religion), so misuse has serious consequences.
items.markingKey: 1 mark could be used to discriminate/harm; 1 mark example or consequence. [2]

items.stem: Explain two ways an organisation can keep personal data secure.
items.answer: Encrypt data so it is unreadable if stolen; use access rights/strong passwords so only authorised staff can see it; firewalls; regular backups; staff training.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark method, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Sunrise Bakery, a bakery in Cape Town, stores names, addresses, dates of birth and payment details of its customers. State two rights that customers have over their personal data.
items.answer: Right to see the data; to have errors corrected; to object to direct marketing; to have data deleted in some cases; to complain to the regulator.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 2. [2]

items.stem: SwiftCar Rentals, a car rental company in Singapore, stores names, addresses, dates of birth and payment details of its customers. (a) Explain why the organisation should not ask for more data than it needs. (b) State two rights that customers have over their personal data.

items.stem: GreenLeaf Pharmacy, a pharmacy in Auckland, stores names, addresses, dates of birth and payment details of its customers. Discuss whether data protection legislation gives enough protection to the customers of GreenLeaf Pharmacy.

items.markingKey: 1 mark for each appropriate action: do not click links in unexpected emails; check the sender; go to the official website directly. [2]

items.stem: Palm Grove Hotel in Hanoi is running an eSafety workshop for students aged 12 to 16. Describe two ways of staying safe when playing online games.
items.answer: Use a nickname; do not share personal information or passwords; use in-game reporting/blocking; be wary of in-game purchase scams; limit chat to friends.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 2. [2]

items.stem: Grace has just joined a social network and an online gaming community, and has asked Northfield Academy in Doha for advice. Discuss whether schools such as Northfield Academy should teach eSafety rather than simply blocking websites.
items.answer: Points for: education gives skills for use at home and on phones; blocking cannot cover everything; students learn to recognise risks. Points against / limitations: blocking provides immediate protection; some students ignore advice; teaching takes time from other subjects. Conclusion: a combination of education and sensible filtering is most effective.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Indicative content — for: education gives skills for use at home and on phones; blocking cannot cover everything; students learn to recognise risks. Against: blocking provides immediate protection; some students ignore advice; teaching takes time from other subjects. Conclusion may argue: a combination of education and sensible filtering is most effective. [4]

items.stem: Explain what is meant by the term 'ergonomics'.
items.answer: Designing equipment and workstations to fit the user, reducing strain and health problems.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Designing equipment and workstations to fit the user, reducing strain and health problems. [2]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Regular breaks reduce the risk of RSI. Reason (R): They stop the same movements being repeated for long periods. Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
items.markingKey: A is true and R explains why A is true.

items.stem: Yusuf works long hours entering data at MetroBus in Singapore. For one health problem, describe its cause and how it can be prevented.
items.answer: e.g. RSI caused by repetitive typing; prevented by breaks, wrist rests, ergonomic keyboard.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cause; 1 mark prevention. [2]

items.stem: Jonas works at Palm Grove Hotel in Madrid and has started to suffer from repetitive strain injury (RSI). Describe a likely cause and two ways it could be prevented.
items.answer: Cause: typing or using a mouse for long periods with the same repeated movements. Prevention: take regular breaks; use an ergonomic keyboard/mouse and wrist rests; correct posture.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cause (typing or using a mouse for long periods with the same repeated movements); 2 marks prevention (take regular breaks; use an ergonomic keyboard/mouse and wrist rests; correct posture). [3]

items.stem: Orbit Games Studio in Lagos has received complaints from office staff about aches and pains. (a) Identify two health problems that can be caused by using computers for long periods. (b) For one health problem, describe its cause and how it can be prevented. (c) Explain how the workstation should be arranged.
items.answer: (a) RSI; eye strain; back/neck problems; headaches; poor circulation. (b) e.g. RSI caused by repetitive typing; prevented by breaks, wrist rests, ergonomic keyboard. (c) Screen at eye level and arm's length; adjustable chair; keyboard and mouse within reach; feet flat; good lighting without glare.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each, max 2. [2] (b) 1 mark cause; 1 mark prevention. [2] (c) 1 mark per point, max 3. [3]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) State what is meant by 'sensitive personal data'. (b) Explain what is meant by the term 'data subject'.
items.answer: (a) Personal data that could be used to discriminate against a person, such as ethnicity, religion, health, political opinions or sexual orientation. (b) The living individual whom personal data is about.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Personal data that could be used to discriminate against a person, such as ethnicity, religion, health, political opinions or sexual orientation. [2] (b) 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: The living individual whom personal data is about. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between 'sensitive personal data' and 'data subject'.
items.answer: sensitive personal data: Personal data that could be used to discriminate against a person, such as ethnicity, religion, health, political opinions or sexual orientation. data subject: The living individual whom personal data is about.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: sensitive personal data correctly described; 1 mark: data subject correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between 'data subject' and 'data controller'.
items.answer: data subject: The living individual whom personal data is about. data controller: The person or organisation that decides why and how personal data is processed and is responsible for complying with data protection law.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: data subject correctly described; 1 mark: data controller correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain two ways an organisation can keep personal data secure. (b) Explain why data protection legislation is needed.
items.answer: (a) Encrypt data so it is unreadable if stolen; use access rights/strong passwords so only authorised staff can see it; firewalls; regular backups; staff training. (b) Organisations hold large amounts of personal data; without rules it could be misused, sold, kept inaccurately or not secured, harming individuals' privacy.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 × (1 mark method, 1 mark explanation). [4] (b) 1 mark large amounts held; 1 mark risk of misuse; 1 mark protects privacy/rights. [3]

items.stem: A school keeps sending reports to an address a family left two years ago, despite being told of the move. Which data protection principle is being broken?
options: Personal data must be accurate and kept up to date
Personal data must not be kept longer than necessary
Personal data must be processed in line with the data subject's rights
Personal data must be kept secure
items.answer: Personal data must be accurate and kept up to date
items.markingKey: Personal data must be accurate and kept up to date.

items.stem: Peak Fitness, a gym chain in Nairobi, stores names, addresses, dates of birth and payment details of its customers. State two rights that customers have over their personal data.
items.answer: Right to see the data; to have errors corrected; to object to direct marketing; to have data deleted in some cases; to complain to the regulator.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 2. [2]

items.stem: Zara has just started working in the records office of Harbour Bank in Dhaka, which holds staff and customer data. (a) Give two examples of personal data the organisation holds. (b) Explain why the organisation should not ask for more data than it needs.
items.answer: (a) Name, address, date of birth, phone number, bank details, medical information. (b) Data must be adequate, relevant and not excessive; extra data increases the harm if there is a breach and costs more to store and protect.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each, max 2. [2] (b) 1 mark principle; 1 mark consequence. [2]

items.stem: Kwame has just started working in the records office of BlueWave Supermarkets in Accra, which holds staff and customer data. Discuss whether data protection legislation gives enough protection to the customers of BlueWave Supermarkets.
items.answer: Points for: sets clear principles; gives individuals rights; fines encourage compliance; requires security. Points against / limitations: laws differ between countries and data crosses borders; breaches still happen; enforcement is slow; people often accept terms without reading them. Conclusion: legislation is necessary but must be backed by good security, enforcement and user awareness.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Indicative content — for: sets clear principles; gives individuals rights; fines encourage compliance; requires security. Against: laws differ between countries and data crosses borders; breaches still happen; enforcement is slow; people often accept terms without reading them. Conclusion may argue: legislation is necessary but must be backed by good security, enforcement and user awareness. [4]

items.stem: Kwame has just started working in the records office of Starlight Cinemas in Lima, which holds staff and customer data. (a) Describe three principles of data protection legislation that the organisation must follow. (b) Explain why the organisation should not ask for more data than it needs.
items.answer: (a) Processed fairly and lawfully; used only for stated purposes; adequate, relevant, not excessive; accurate and up to date; not kept longer than necessary; processed in line with subjects' rights; kept secure; not transferred abroad without adequate protection. (b) Data must be adequate, relevant and not excessive; extra data increases the harm if there is a breach and costs more to store and protect.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each, max 3. [3] (b) 1 mark principle; 1 mark consequence. [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Define the term 'eSafety'. (b) State what is meant by 'cyberbullying'.
items.answer: (a) Using the internet and digital devices in a way that protects your personal safety, privacy and wellbeing. (b) Using digital technology, such as social media or messaging, to threaten, embarrass or harass another person.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Using the internet and digital devices in a way that protects your personal safety, privacy and wellbeing. [2] (b) 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Using digital technology, such as social media or messaging, to threaten, embarrass or harass another person. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between 'privacy settings' and 'grooming'.
items.answer: privacy settings: Settings on social media or apps that control who can see a user's posts and personal information. grooming: When a person builds an online relationship with a young person in order to exploit or abuse them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: privacy settings correctly described; 1 mark: grooming correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Describe the difference between 'grooming' and 'eSafety'.
items.answer: grooming: When a person builds an online relationship with a young person in order to exploit or abuse them. eSafety: Using the internet and digital devices in a way that protects your personal safety, privacy and wellbeing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: grooming correctly described; 1 mark: eSafety correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: A student wants to meet someone they have only chatted to online. Describe what the user should do to stay safe.
items.answer: Do not meet online contacts alone; tell a trusted adult; meet in a public place with an adult if at all.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each appropriate action: do not meet online contacts alone; tell a trusted adult; meet in a public place with an adult if at all. [2]

items.stem: MetroBus in Seoul is running an eSafety workshop for students aged 12 to 16. Explain the risks of meeting someone in person who was met online.
items.answer: They may not be who they say (grooming); risk of abuse or harm; should tell an adult and meet in a public place with an adult.
items.markingKey: 1 mark risk; 1 mark explanation/precaution. [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain what is meant by the term 'ergonomics'. (b) State what is meant by 'eye strain'.
items.answer: (a) Designing equipment and workstations to fit the user, reducing strain and health problems. (b) Tired, sore or dry eyes and blurred vision caused by looking at a screen for long periods without breaks.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Regular breaks reduce the risk of RSI. Reason (R): Reflections on the screen make the eyes work harder. Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
items.markingKey: A and R are both true statements, but R does not explain A.

items.stem: Ana works at Starlight Cinemas in Cape Town and has started to suffer from eye strain. Describe a likely cause and two ways it could be prevented.
items.answer: Cause: looking at a screen for long periods, glare or flickering screens. Prevention: take regular breaks and look into the distance; use anti-glare screens; adjust brightness; have eye tests.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cause (looking at a screen for long periods, glare or flickering screens); 2 marks prevention (take regular breaks and look into the distance; use anti-glare screens; adjust brightness; have eye tests). [3]
